answer.rationale: Timeline fit points at the release: latency began climbing ~90 minutes ago, the release shipped ~2 hours ago, and memory_b6 confirms this codebase has shipped regressions that only surface post-deploy. Rollback (memory_b1) is the only candidate that addresses a suspected cause rather than a symptom. Regional failover is excluded outright: memory_b2 is the one inherited record that carries its own failure mode -- a 40-minute replication gap and two lost writes -- with the explicit constraint 'never fail over while writes are hot.' Settlement writes are at daily peak, so that constraint is live and binding against the primary objective of not losing customer writes. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked as pre-provisioned headroom ahead of a known peak, not as a mid-incident remedy, and provisioning lag likely exceeds the incident window. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained a third-party partner outage; there is no external dependency signal here, so it would shed our own settlement writes to mask an internal regression. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) is the safest non-destructive fallback and is why I am spending a verification pull on it: if the archived record shows the day-55 write-path recovery came from genuine primary offload rather than coincident load decay, it becomes a viable no-write-risk option should rollback be contraindicated. I am verifying memory_b1 because it is the record my intended action rests on entirely, and its summary is suspiciously clean -- note that every inherited memory except b2 has been compressed to a success-only narrative, which is a consolidation bias, not evidence of risk-free actions. Specifically I need the original record to check whether the day-18 rollback involved schema or data-format migrations. Rolling back a build that has been writing new-format settlement records for two hours at peak volume could itself destroy or orphan customer writes -- the exact harm I am trying to prevent. If b1 shows the prior rollback was schema-neutral and the current release carries no forward migration, I proceed. Scale is a small guarded test: roll back a bounded slice of write traffic first to confirm the causal link before full reversion, because the release-correlation is temporal, not proven, and a full peak-hour reversion on an unverified hypothesis is the larger risk. If latency does not respond on the guarded slice, the release is not the cause and I hold for the next window rather than spending the intervention on failover.
